newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE-Families wait in hope for Sri Lanka's miss.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Families wait in hope for Sri Lanka's miss.

text.p: Druki Martenstyn's bungalow is dominated by her husband's hunting trophies and bric-a-brac.
Antlers and oil paintings line the walls while an elephant's foot competes for space on the floor with elegant colonial furniture, cases jammed with rare books and piles of magazines.
"You see, my husband is a collector," she explains.
But Martenstyn hasn't seen her husband for over 18 months.

Cedric Martenstyn is one of around 2,000 Sri Lankan soldiers, navy and airmen who are missing in action (MIA), lost in the long-running ethnic war between the government in Colombo and separatists of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).
A naval commander, his MI17 helicopter was shot down in January 1996 over the sea near Point Pedro on the northern Jaffna peninsula, which Sri Lankan troops had just recaptured.
Military sources blamed the attack on the LTTE, which is fighting for a homeland for the minority Tamil population in the north and east of the Indian Ocean island.
But no one claimed responsibility for the incident and the fate of the passengers was never clear.
Witnesses said they saw people jump into the sea from the helicopter and Sri Lankan military intelligence reported sightings of a man fitting Cedric's description held by guerrillas in a jungle camp.
LIFE IN LIMBO
So his wife lives on in hope, waiting for news and convinced, like so many others, that her husband will return.
And like the others, a large part of her life has been frozen, held in aspic until the head of the family returns.
"We are left in limbo," says Druki Martenstyn, with a fixed smile.
"As long as there is a hope of return, no one will take that role. People need a body and a funeral before saying goodbye."

Unable to cope alone and unwilling to admit defeat, Martenstyn sought out other women in a similar position and with their help formed a support organisation, which she says has helped her deal with the trauma of uncertainty and loss.
They set up the Association for Families of Servicemen Missing in Action (AFSMIA) and advertised in newspapers for other MIA families.
"The response was overwhelming," said Chiranga Palihena, whose husband was on board the same helicopter when it was shot down. "Over 800 letters from all over the country...Terrible stories."
Funded by voluntary donations, AFSMIA offers support to families of MIAs and helps them get in touch with doctors and government bodies that can give them specialist help.
MIA FAMILIES FACE SPECIAL PROBLEMS

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) says the families of MIAs have to deal with special problems, which are not usually faced by the relations of the more than 50,000 killed in the ethnic war.
"They need to know if someone is dead or alive in order to get on with their lives. They undergo trauma," said Harasha Gunewardena, spokesman for the ICRC in Colombo.
Many of the families' problems are financial.
The Sri Lankan government pays a modest sum of some 50,000 to 100,000 rupees ($850-$1,700) in war compensation to next of kin, but this is paid out quickly only if death is confirmed.
If there is any evidence the men may be alive, nothing is paid for a year, sometimes leaving families without an income.

"Many of these men were supporting their families. Suddenly they are penniless. And even if the money comes, the problems don't end. If the wife gets the salary, the man's parents may get nothing, leaving them penniless," said Martenstyn.
"We've also heard of cases where the in-laws have taken the money and the wives have ended up with nothing. We have suicides."
FEW PRISONERS TAKEN
Martenstyn says AFSMIA attempts to help get information about men and tries not to give false hope to the families.
But some government and aid officials feel the group may be doing just that. While welcoming AFSMIA's efforts, they suggest the rebels take very few prisoners.
"The chances of most of these MIAs being alive are very slim," said one official, who declined to be identified.
"The LTTE is a guerrilla force, moving around constantly. They don't control a fixed place and it would be logistically very difficult to have a large number of prisoners," he said.
The ICRC declined to comment on the fate of MIAs but said it had access to only 25 prisoners in LTTE custody.
Whatever the officials say, Martenstyn and hundreds of women like her refuse to accept that their loved ones may not return.
"There's not a moment of the day when I don't think of my son's return," said AFSMIA founder-member Purangani Goonewardene. "In the dark, at night, I know he is alive."
($1 = 58.8 rupees)
